style.style_summary: A Korean LoL gameplay commentary short: vertically cropped 16:9 gameplay (letterboxed with black bars top and bottom) plays as long, uncut takes, driven entirely by burned-in narration subtitles that swap every 1–2 seconds. The only real 'edits' are a mid-video meme interlude — a full-bleed crying-cat-with-Gnar-hat image versus a menacing Darkin/Aatrox splash — joined by dip-to-black fades, used as a visual punchline for the 'cute but terrifying' commentary point. It ends on a self-deprecating caption gag and fades out on the action.
style.hook_technique: No title card or pre-roll: it opens mid-teamfight with damage numbers and health bars already popping, and the first subtitle lands within the first half second on a curiosity-baiting descriptive claim ('has a cute appearance...'), forcing viewers to stay for the contradicting second half of the sentence.
style.pacing: Visually slow-cut, verbally fast: the gameplay segments (0–19s, 27–34s) are essentially uninterrupted single takes with zero hard cuts, while subtitle lines change every ~1–2s to keep perceived pace high. The mid-roll meme insert holds each still 2–3s (cat ~19–21.5s, Aatrox ~22–24s, composite cat ~24.5–26.5s) with ~0.5–1s dip-to-black fades between them, creating a deliberate rhythm break before returning to gameplay.
style.caption_style: Single-line (occasionally two-word) Korean subtitles in bold white sans-serif with a soft dark translucent plate behind them, centered horizontally and parked in the lower-third above the HUD so the minimap/item bar stays readable. Each line is one spoken clause, held 1–2s, sometimes repeated across two shots; short reaction captions ('아..', '손이 미끄러졌네..') are used as comedic beats. No emojis, no on-screen titles, no captions at all during the meme interlude.
style.structure: 1) Cold open into live teamfight with the thesis subtitle. 2) 0–19s continuous gameplay while narration explains the champion's nerfed/weak state, caption-by-caption. 3) 17–19s escalation to the 'solo kill' payoff, captions drop out to let the action breathe. 4) 19–27s meme interlude: crying cat = cute version, fade to black, Darkin splash = scary version, fade, cat+Gnar composite — a silent visual joke restating the commentary. 5) 27–34s return to gameplay for the aftermath, capped by a self-deprecating punchline caption and a fade to black mid-action.
learned_rules: Open cold on the highest-action moment of the clip and place the first subtitle line within the first 0.5 seconds, phrased as an incomplete claim that only resolves in the next line.
Keep gameplay in long uncut takes and generate pace with subtitle turnover instead of cuts — swap one short caption line every 1–2 seconds, one spoken clause per line.
Burn captions as bold white text on a soft dark translucent plate, centered in the lower third and above the game HUD, never covering the minimap or item bar.
Letterbox the 16:9 gameplay in a 9:16 frame and keep the crop centered on the champion so the black bars double as caption space.
Insert one silent full-bleed meme/still interlude in the middle (around the 55–70% mark) that visually restates the narration's joke, holding each still 2–3 seconds.
Join interlude stills with 0.5–1s dip-to-black fades rather than hard cuts, and drop all captions during the interlude so the image carries the gag.
Return to gameplay after the interlude and end on a short self-deprecating reaction caption over live action, fading to black mid-play instead of using an outro card.

style.style_summary: A Korean LoL 'champion guide' short built entirely from vertically cropped gameplay footage with voiceover narration. There are no transitions, zooms, or music-driven flourishes — the entire edit rhythm lives in (a) jump cuts between gameplay moments and (b) burned-in two-line subtitles that swap precisely on each spoken clause. A fixed champion portrait sits top-center the whole video as a branding/topic anchor, and the game HUD is deliberately kept visible so viewers can read gold/level/items as supporting evidence. Footage is chosen so that what happens on screen literally demonstrates the sentence being said, and it escalates chronologically from lane phase to late-game snowball.
style.hook_technique: Opens with zero preamble: a claim-style thesis caption ('탑 후반 밸류 최강자인 문도입니다') appears on frame 1 over already-in-progress teamfight action, with the champion icon pinned top-center so the subject is identified instantly. The hook is a strong opinion + immediate visual proof, no intro logo, no self-introduction.
style.pacing: Steady, narration-led. Gameplay shots run roughly 3–5s each (cuts detectable at ~3s, ~6s, ~13s, ~16s, ~21s, ~25s, ~31s, ~36s, ~41s, ~46s), and each cut lands on a sentence boundary rather than on a beat. Within a shot the frame keeps moving because the camera follows the player, so no shot ever feels static. Density is uniform — no slow intro, no sped-up montage — and there are ~14 caption blocks over 56s, i.e. one text beat every ~3.5s.
style.caption_style: Bold white Korean sans-serif with a heavy dark outline/drop shadow, centered, sitting in the lower third just above the game HUD. Max two lines, line-broken at natural phrase boundaries (e.g. '초반엔 파밍 위주로 / 하는 게 좋지만'), roughly 8–16 characters per line. Captions are hard-cut in/out with no animation, appear and vanish exactly with the spoken clause, and are intentionally blank for 0.5–1.5s during pauses or when the game itself shows a banner ('적을 처치했습니다!', 'ONE TOP DESTROYED', level-up) so the on-screen game text can be read without collision.
style.structure: 1) Thesis hook (0–3s): 'this champion is the strongest late-game top'. 2) Early-game caveat (3–10s): farming-first advice illustrated by lane trading clips. 3) Problem beat (10–17s): getting punished in lane, matchup-dependent trades, with a kill/level-up moment. 4) Turn (17–31s): 'if a late-game champ gets ahead early there's no answer' — escalating skirmish footage plus a scoreboard cut as data proof, ending on a kill. 5) Payoff (31–46s): late-game item-diff clips, tower kill and shutdown banners as climax. 6) Closing generalization (46–56s): 'mages suffer especially' over a late-game duel, functioning as a takeaway line instead of a CTA.
learned_rules: Cut the footage only on sentence/clause boundaries so every shot change coincides with a new narration line, keeping shots around 3–5 seconds.
Swap subtitles exactly on the spoken clause boundary and hold each caption 2–4 seconds — never let text linger past the audio or appear before it.
Limit each caption to two lines of ~8–16 characters, breaking lines at natural grammatical phrase points instead of mid-phrase.
Place bold white text with a heavy dark outline in the lower third, above the game HUD, and never cover the HUD or scoreboard.
Insert deliberate 0.5–1.5s caption gaps during narration pauses and whenever the game displays its own banner (kill, tower, level-up) so the on-screen event reads cleanly.
Pin a fixed subject anchor (champion/topic icon) at top-center for the entire video as a constant identity cue.
Choose footage that literally demonstrates the sentence being narrated, and order clips chronologically from early game to late game so the argument escalates.
Open on frame one with a bold thesis caption over mid-action footage — no intro, no logo, no self-introduction.
End on a takeaway generalization caption over a final decisive clip rather than an outro card.

style.style_summary: A cinematic movie-recap edit built entirely from tight close-ups of two characters, cut in a shot/reverse-shot dialogue rhythm. Footage is heavily zoomed and slow push-in scaled (each shot slowly enlarges over its duration), color-graded toward a unified magenta/purple wash so cuts feel continuous. The real engine is the subtitle layer: one short Korean line at a time, vertically centered around the lower-middle third, with the text color changed per speaker/emotion (yellow for main narration, blue-white for the other voice, red for warnings, green for magical/spell beats, gray-white for narrator asides) and a soft glow/shadow behind it so it reads over busy faces. A separate persistent lyric watermark ('BURN IT UP') sits at the bottom, signalling a music bed under the whole clip.
style.hook_technique: Opens mid-action on the most recognizable image (bloodied hero mid-fight) with no intro card, and the first caption states the premise as an unresolved setup — '스파이더맨의 정체가' / '밝혀지자' — splitting one sentence across two shots so the viewer must stay for the payoff, then immediately hard-cuts to a question line ('모두가 절 잊으면요?') and a reaction close-up within 3 seconds.
style.pacing: Steady 1–2s average shot length in the first half (cuts land on nearly every caption change, ~0.8–1.5s), with dialogue exchanges alternating faces every beat; the middle emotional section stretches to 2–3s holds on a single face while captions swap inside the shot; the final 4–5s slows further to near-static close-ups with sparse text for the emotional landing. No transitions — all hard cuts, motion supplied by slow digital zoom within each shot.
style.caption_style: Single short line, bold rounded Korean sans-serif, 1 line max (~6–10 characters or one clause), centered horizontally and placed at roughly 50–55% height (over the chest/chin, never covering eyes). Color-coded by speaker and mood: warm yellow = protagonist/narrator, pale blue = the other character, red = threat/refusal, green = spell/magic lines, off-white = neutral narration. Every line carries a soft dark blur-glow or drop shadow so it stays legible on any frame. Text appears/disappears exactly on the syllable it is spoken, and a repeated line is re-shown across a cut rather than removed.
style.structure: 1) 0–3s cold-open hook: action close-up + split setup sentence. 2) 3–13s rapid dialogue volley (request/refusal) with shot-reverse-shot and speaker-colored captions. 3) 13–23s escalation: red 'no' beat, then the emotional warning delivered in one long-held close-up with sequential captions. 4) 23–33s narrator-voiced turn (neutral white text) explaining the sacrifice, slower cuts. 5) 33–41s emotional resolution: quiet thank-you exchange, longest holds, final smile close-up as the button — no CTA, no outro card.
learned_rules: Cut on every caption change so each new line of text lands on a new shot or a new push-in, keeping average shot length under 2 seconds in the first 15 seconds.
Show only one short line of text at a time, centered horizontally at about 50–55% of frame height, and never let it cover the subject's eyes.

Assign a fixed caption color per speaker or emotion (e.g. yellow=protagonist, blue=other voice, red=threat/refusal, green=magic-or-twist, white=narrator) and keep that mapping consistent for the whole video.
Add a soft dark glow or drop shadow behind all captions so bold text stays readable over bright, busy close-ups.
Time caption in/out points to the exact syllable of the audio, and if a line continues past a cut, carry the same text across the cut instead of retyping it.
Open cold on the most recognizable action close-up and split the premise sentence across the first two shots so the payoff arrives only after the second cut.
Grade all clips to one dominant color wash and use slow digital zoom inside each static shot so hard cuts feel like one continuous scene.
Slow the cut rate to 2–3 second holds for the emotional turn and end on a single quiet close-up with no outro card or CTA.

style.style_summary: A movie-clip recut (Spider-Man 2) edited as a rapid-fire montage of 'life falling apart' beats. Every line of dialogue is retranslated into short, punchy Korean subtitles placed at face level, color-coded by emotional charge (yellow = neutral/complaint, green = sarcastic/soft, red = harsh/verdict lines like '해고야'). Cuts land on the punchline of each line, with a white flash-frame used as a hard transition/beat marker. Underlying music ('BURN IT UP') keeps a constant driving pulse, and the original burned-in music-label caption sits at the bottom while the Korean text does all narrative work.
style.hook_technique: Opens mid-conflict with zero setup: a close-up smiling face, then an immediate cut to an accusing line ('늦었네요') within ~1 second, followed by escalating rejection lines ('돈 못 드려요' → '넌 해고야, 나가' → '해고야' → '자넨 해고됐어'). The hook is a stacked repetition of the same devastating word across three different characters, in bright red, capped by a white flash frame at ~8.5s that resets attention before the story body.
style.pacing: Very fast and metronomic: most shots run 0.8–1.5s in the first 10s (one shot per subtitle line), a brief 2s breathing shot for emotional beats (grandma scenes, 20–22s and 27–35s hold the same caption over 2 shots), then tightening again. Roughly 35–45 cuts in 52s. Cuts are dialogue-driven, not visual-driven; a white flash and a whip-blur cut are used at structural pivots (8.5s, 24.5s, 45.5s). Ends on a wide, caption-free room shot for a quiet 3–4s release.
style.caption_style: Single-line Korean sentences, bold rounded sans-serif, always centered horizontally at mouth/chin height over the face so eyes stay readable. Heavy dark soft-glow/blur behind the text instead of a solid box, giving contrast on any background. Color as meaning: yellow for narration/neutral gripes, lime green for sarcastic or gentle lines, red for verdict/shock words, pale blue for resigned lines; within a line, the key noun is colored differently from the rest (e.g. '스파이더맨의' red + rest white, '20달러로' red + rest white) to spotlight the payload word. Captions persist across 2 shots when a single line spans two cuts, and asterisked labels (*압류 통보*) are used for on-screen prop explanation.
style.structure: 1) 0–8s hook: rapid stack of firing/rejection lines from multiple characters, each 1s. 2) 8.5s white-flash reset. 3) 9–22s escalation montage: getting hit, dropped books, late for class, falling grades — one line per shot. 4) 22–25s turn: friend's question + *압류 통보* prop insert as a stakes bump. 5) 26–35s emotional dip with slower cuts (aunt giving money, tears). 6) 36–47s relationship + rent punchlines, colored key words. 7) 48–52s caption-free wide shot outro that lets the music and image land with no text.
learned_rules: Cut on every completed spoken line so one subtitle equals one shot, keeping most shots between 0.8 and 1.5 seconds.
Stack three to four escalating variations of the same shocking phrase in the first 8 seconds before any context is given.
Color-code subtitles by emotion — red for verdicts and shocks, yellow for neutral narration, green for sarcasm or softness, blue for resignation — and never use more than one color meaning per line.
Recolor only the single key noun or number inside a line (price, name, verdict word) so the payload word pops out of the sentence.
Place all captions centered at mouth/chin height with a soft dark glow behind the text instead of a solid box, and keep each line to one short readable clause.
Insert a one-beat white flash frame (or whip blur) at each structural pivot to reset attention between hook, body, and turn.
Hold the same caption across two consecutive shots on emotional beats to slow the perceived rhythm without stopping the cuts.
End on a wide, caption-free shot for the final 3–4 seconds so the music and image resolve without text.
